title: Beads and silence
hook: Catholics pray the rosary and keep adoration before the sacrament; the Catholic path goes deeper
tomorrow: camp 3 close: a rule of life

segments.voice: Yesterday: confession and anointing, words of absolution and healing oil. Your line was said out loud, it loosens. Did something loosen? Day one hundred fifty-five.

Watch an elderly woman in the back pew of a Catholic church on a weekday afternoon. The church is nearly empty. Her lips are moving, barely. And in her hands, a loop of small beads slides, one at a time, through her fingers. She isn't reading. She's not looking at anything in particular. Her fingers know the way, the way your fingers know a zipper or a phone code. Maybe she's praying for a grandson. Maybe she's just resting. Many Catholics have seen a grandmother do this. Some have seen a rosary tucked into a coffin, or hanging from a rearview mirror. Today's word is that loop of beads, and what it does with a restless pair of hands.
screen: `AN EMPTY CHURCH, A WEEKDAY.` → `BEADS SLIDING THROUGH HER FINGERS.` → `HER HANDS KNOW THE WAY.`

segments.voice: Rosary. From the Latin rosarium, a rose garden: a garland of prayers. The rosary is a string of beads grouped in tens, called decades. On each large bead, a person prays the Our Father. On each of the ten small beads, a Hail Mary. Then a short prayer of praise, Glory be to the Father. Five decades make a usual rosary. The Hail Mary begins with the angel's greeting to Mary in Luke's gospel, in the Catholic Douay-Rheims Bible: "Hail, full of grace, the Lord is with thee: blessed art thou among women." It goes on with words from her cousin Elizabeth and a request for Mary's prayers. But the words are only half of it. While the lips repeat, the mind walks slowly through scenes from the lives of Jesus and Mary, called the mysteries: the joyful ones, like the birth in Bethlehem; the sorrowful ones, like the cross; the glorious ones, like the resurrection. In 2002, Pope John Paul the Second added a fourth set, the luminous mysteries, from Jesus's public life. The repetition isn't meant to be boring. It's like waves: the words settle the body so the heart can look. Then there's the silence. Many Catholics keep adoration: sitting quietly in a chapel before the consecrated bread of the Eucharist, displayed on the altar, sometimes for an hour, sometimes through the night, taking turns. No words needed. Orthodox Christians use a knotted prayer rope with the Jesus Prayer. Some Anglicans and Lutherans use prayer beads too. Most Protestants don't pray the rosary, because they don't address prayers to Mary, and many pray without beads at all. For the Catholics who use them, the beads keep the hands busy so the heart can be still. The Catholic path on Infinite Hill goes much deeper into both.
screen: `ROSARIUM — A GARLAND OF ROSES.` · `DECADES: ONE OUR FATHER, TEN HAIL MARYS.` · `THE LIPS REPEAT, THE HEART LOOKS.` · `ADORATION: SILENCE BEFORE THE SACRAMENT.` · then, large: `HAIL, FULL OF GRACE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice. Find something small to hold. A rosary or prayer rope if you have one. If not, a smooth stone, a ring, a button, even your own fingers, one at a time. Let your hand hold it and move slowly. With each small movement, one breath. If you pray, you can let each breath carry a short prayer you already know, or just a name. If you don't, let the object anchor you here. Notice how busy hands can quiet a busy head. The bell holds the time.
Rosary. Latin for a rose garden: a loop of beads, decades of prayer, and scenes from the lives of Jesus and Mary.
Your line: the hands can pray too. Today, hold something in your hand while you pray or sit still for a minute. Day one hundred fifty-five.

howItsDone: Many Catholics pray the rosary daily or weekly, alone or in groups, and some keep an hour of silent adoration before the Eucharist; Orthodox Christians often pray the Jesus Prayer on a knotted prayer rope, and some Anglicans and Lutherans use prayer beads.

fork.setup: you're an Orthodox Christian with a knotted prayer rope. on each knot, what do you most likely pray?
fork.reveal: the Jesus Prayer: Lord Jesus Christ, Son of God, have mercy on me. the rope, like the rosary, keeps the hands praying.

original.note: Latin: a rose garden, a garland of roses. the English word rosary comes from it.

trapdoor: what you thought: a rosary is a necklace of beads.
what it means: a way of praying with the hands: decades of prayers while the heart walks through scenes from the lives of Jesus and Mary.
what a scholar hears: the rosary grew gradually in the Middle Ages from repeated psalms and prayers; tradition links it to Saint Dominic. John Paul II added the luminous mysteries in 2002.

notes: Douay-Rheims (Challoner) Luke 1:28: 'Hail, full of grace, the Lord is with thee: blessed art thou among women.' Confirm exact wording.
Rosary structure (Our Father on large beads, ten Hail Marys, Glory Be, five decades; introductory prayers omitted). Confirm simplification.
History: gradual development; the tradition linking it to St Dominic is presented as tradition. Confirm.
Adoration described as the consecrated host displayed (monstrance) with people taking turns (perpetual adoration). Confirm.
Protestant position ('don't address prayers to Mary') is a generalization; confirm tone is neutral.
The Jesus Prayer wording in the fork is the common form (also taught on day 99). Confirm.
